cards.front: Why must a chemical carry the signal across a synapse instead of the action potential itself?
cards.back: An action potential cannot jump the **synaptic cleft**, the narrow gap between two cells, so a neurotransmitter carries the message across.
cards.hint: Think about where an action potential exists: in the membrane of a single neurone.

cards.front: What are the steps by which an action potential at the synaptic knob releases neurotransmitter?
cards.back: 1) The action potential opens voltage-gated $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ channels in the presynaptic membrane. 2) $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ diffuse into the knob. 3) Vesicles move to the membrane and fuse with it. 4) Contents are released by **exocytosis**.

cards.front: How does neurotransmitter binding start a new impulse in the postsynaptic neurone?
cards.back: It binds to **receptor proteins** that form part of sodium ion channels, opening them. $\text{Na}^{+}$ diffuse in and depolarise the membrane; if threshold is reached, an action potential starts.
cards.hint: Think about which ions move, and which way, when a channel opens.

cards.back: The **synaptic cleft** is the narrow fluid-filled gap between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes at a synapse.
A **neurotransmitter** is a chemical released at a synapse that binds to receptors on the receiving cell. Acetylcholine is one example.
cards.hint: Think about the substance stored inside the vesicles in the presynaptic knob.

cards.front: What is a receptor protein at a synapse?
cards.back: A **receptor protein** is a protein in the postsynaptic membrane with a binding site complementary to one specific neurotransmitter.
cards.hint: Think about why a key only fits one lock.

cards.front: What does the enzyme acetylcholinesterase do in the synaptic cleft?
cards.back: It **hydrolyses** acetylcholine into choline and ethanoic acid, so the signal stops quickly and each impulse gives a short, precise signal.
cards.hint: Think about what must happen to a neurotransmitter once it has bound.

cards.front: What happens to the products of acetylcholine breakdown after they are formed in the cleft?
cards.back: They are taken back into the presynaptic knob, where ATP is used to make acetylcholine again.
cards.hint: Think about which cell the breakdown products return to.

cards.front: Why must neurotransmitter be removed from the synaptic cleft after it has acted?
cards.back: If it stayed, receptors would stay occupied and sodium channels would stay open, so the postsynaptic neurone would keep firing and the signal could not be controlled.

cards.front: Why can a synapse only pass signals in one direction?
cards.back: Vesicles of neurotransmitter occur only in the presynaptic knob, and receptor proteins only in the postsynaptic membrane, so the signal cannot pass back.
cards.hint: Compare where the chemical is stored with where it is detected.

cards.front: What is summation at a synapse?
cards.back: **Summation** is the adding together of neurotransmitter effects from several impulses in quick succession, bringing the postsynaptic membrane to threshold when one impulse alone might not.
cards.hint: Think about what happens if a single signal is too weak to reach threshold.

cards.front: What does an inhibitory synapse do to the postsynaptic membrane?
cards.back: It makes the membrane **more negative**, so an action potential becomes less likely.
cards.hint: Compare this with what happens when the membrane depolarises.

cards.front: Why does a synaptic knob contain many mitochondria?
cards.back: They supply **ATP** to move vesicles to the membrane and to make neurotransmitter again from its breakdown products.
cards.hint: Think about the energy-demanding jobs done inside the knob.
